Although the need for a building program in the Hardin districts is primarily a result of growth from coal development, the net effect has not been entirely detrimental. Because the mine lies within district boundaries, district levies are applied to the coal and revenues obtained have approximately equaled costs. The net impact of coal on the school districts has been neutral; those districts which have experienced enrollment increases from the coal have also experienced increased taxable valuation of similar magnitude (Big Horn County Superintendent of Schools, personal communication, January 8, 1976).
Attempts to Locate Alternative Sources of Funding -The several jurisdictions in the impact area are becoming increasingly aware of potential outside sources of revenue to help finance their responses to coalrelated impacts. Only Hardin and the school districts which serve it will experience negative fiscal impacts from coal development by Westmoreland, and these jurisdictions are carefully investigating sources of funding to alleviate some of the budget strains brought about by coal development and the associated in-migration of workers.
Hardin's efforts to discover alternative sources of funding have been considerable. In 1975, the city and county were jointly awarded a two year grant from the Old West Regional Commission to support a full-time person whose basic duties are to locate and apply for grants of many types. The position is set up to help all government bodies within the county, including the school districts. Rusty Rokita, who filled this position, has been concentrating on obtaining monies available through the Coal Board, and a potential grant from the EPA.
